articleSummary: Anvisa authorizes Flyttr (formerly Oxitec) to produce and supply Wolbachia-infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in Brazil, adding a second private supplier to the technology. Wolbachia, a bacterium naturally found in about 50–60% of insects, is not present in Aedes aegypti by default. The 2008 Monash University technique inserts Wolbachia into mosquito eggs in the lab; inside the insect, it blocks viral replication, lowering viral loads and slowing transmission of dengue, Zika, and chikungunya. Infected mosquitoes are released to spread the trait locally, with no risk to humans or other mammals. Trials began in Brazil in 2012, with Niterói, Rio de Janeiro, as a pioneer; large-scale urban deployments began in 2014. Ministry indicators report dengue down 69.4%, chikungunya down 56.3%, and Zika down 37%.

articleHeadline: Có nên tiêm vaccine phòng bệnh sốt xuất huyết?
articleSummary: Vietnam faces ongoing dengue fever, especially during the rainy season in dense urban areas. Dengue virus, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, has four serotypes (DEN-1 to DEN-4); infection with a different serotype can cause reinfection and sometimes more severe disease. WHO notes global dengue cases rising; there is no specific antiviral, so prevention relies on mosquito control and supportive care. The qdenga vaccine (Takeda, Japan) is licensed in many countries and has been deployed in Vietnam, targeting all four serotypes and shown to reduce symptomatic dengue, hospitalizations, and severe outcomes. It is approved for individuals aged 4 years and older, including those with or without prior dengue infection, with no pre-vaccination serology required; a two-dose schedule is given 3 months apart. Vaccination should be complemented by vector control. Cautions include acute illness, pregnancy, immune suppression, and prior severe vaccine reactions; pre-vaccination screening is advised.

The white-striped mosquito, Aedes albopictus, enters the annual high-activity peak, raising concerns for dengue fever and chikungunya; Culex tritaeniorhynchus remains a vector for Japanese encephalitis, and Anopheles sinensis for malaria. The forecast combines data from 16 city monitoring stations, historical weather, and forecasts. Prevention emphasizes source reduction and personal protection: wear light-colored long sleeves and pants, apply DEET or Picaridin repellents, and avoid dawn/dusk outdoors—especially for infants, pregnant women, the elderly, and those with underlying diseases. Check and eliminate standing water daily in high-risk areas (every 3 days elsewhere); use screens and nets; seek medical care if fever, headache, joint pain, or rash and provide travel history. Source: Shandong CDC.

articleHeadline: Ebola : le ministre congolais de la Santé à Kampala pour coordonner la riposte avec l'Ouganda
articleSummary: Congolese Health Minister Samuel-Roger Kamba arrived in Kampala to strengthen cross-border cooperation with Uganda against Ebola, focusing on border-area surveillance, prevention, and urgent-response coordination. The Bundibugyo strain, originating in Ituri, has crossed into Uganda with about twenty cases and two deaths. As of mid-July, Uganda is approaching the end of its outbreak, with no new confirmed cases since June 21 and a 42-day countdown begun July 16 to end-of-outbreak declaration; Congo's outbreak continues, with over 2,260 cases and nearly 900 deaths. The two countries seek to prevent re-importation and leverage Ugandan response experience for Congo's response. African CDC urges early detection, transparent information sharing, and regional coordination; WHO cautions that border closures hinder control and stigmatization.

articleHeadline: Ebola en RDC : le cap des 1 000 morts franchi, 2 536 cas confirmés au 21 juillet
articleSummary: As of July 21, Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo reached 1,033 deaths from 2,536 confirmed cases (case-fatality 40.7%), with Ituri accounting for 88.6% of cases (2,248 cases, 864 deaths). The Bundibugyo strain drives the outbreak across five provinces—Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Tshopo and Haut-Uele—with 47 health zones (46 in active transmission). Haut-Uele reports 21 cases and 12 deaths; diagnostic testing began there. North Kivu has the highest fatality at 58.7% (152/259). Unlike the Zaïre strain, Bundibugyo has no approved vaccine or specific treatment; control relies on screening, isolation, contact tracing, safe burials, and clinical care. National bed occupancy is 86.9%; North Kivu centers operate at 129.1% capacity (182 patients for 141 beds). Ituri’s contact tracing stands at 75.4%. Over 14 laboratories yield 24-hour results; government has allocated $50 million. Challenges include post-mortem sampling reluctance, insecurity, provider strikes, and shortages. AfDB pledges $13 million for the region.
notes: Bundibugyo株はワクチン・特効薬が未承認であり、Zaïre株流行時とは対応が異なる点に留意。病床占有率が高く（一部129%）、医療体制逼迫と治安不安、医療従事者ストライキが管理可能性に影響。AfDBや政府予算の投入があるが国際支援の継続的必要性が高い。

articleHeadline: As Ebola Spreads In DRC, Past Outbreaks Provide Map For Success
articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is expanding, with 1,708 confirmed cases and 580 deaths as of July 8, 2026. No approved vaccines or treatments exist for the Bundibugyo variant; diagnostic tests detect only common strains, and blood samples must be sent about 1,500 kilometers to Kinshasa, causing dayslong delays in confirmation and response. The outbreak began in May and could last up to a year, with officials noting the expansion phase. Barriers include armed-group violence (e.g., M23), mass displacement exceeding 5 million people, food insecurity, and strained health infrastructure. Community engagement is deemed essential, drawing on lessons from the 2014 West Africa outbreak and a 2025 DRC outbreak to build trust, support contact tracing, vaccination, and treatment. Kasai province saw 64 infections and 45 deaths in three months during a Sept 2025 outbreak; WHO data in June 2026 emphasized community-centered response.
